stories.description: Once a strictly US affair, it's become a truly global phenomenon. From shoppers hunting for bargains in Louisiana, to queues forming outside stores in Venezuela, the Black Friday sales event has become the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic. stories.description: Net migration fell in the year ending June 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler . Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero. Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services. The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level. British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. stories.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
stories.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. stories.title: I asked AI if it was OK to use AI to write an obituary. The answer surprised me | Anna Spargo-Ryan
stories.description: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her. The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’. That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out. Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired? Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally. “We must investigate these actions. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA IV’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. stories.description: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes Sign up to the Breaking News US email Nvidia ’s shares have surged by 31% at the start of trading following the news. Here’s Trump ’s full social media post, in which he also called Jensen Huang “a Great Patriot and National Treasure”. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. stories.title: Dylan Moran goes looking for trouble and disappears off the beaten track in this baffling comedy show
stories.description: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

stories.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
stories.description: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and growing defence ambitions Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday. That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election. Cop 31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded. Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack , causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel. Weapons | The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons. UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal. West Bank | Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank after dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday. Monday | FIFA is set to announce that the UK will host the 2035 Women’s World Cup. Thursday | RMT will begin a series of eight 24-hour strikes on the London Underground over the next three months due to a dispute over a four-day week for its drivers. Sunday | Spain will hold snap parliamentary elections in what will be the country’s sixth general election in 11 years. Continue reading...

stories.description: President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China. But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today. This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state. It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink. During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP. “We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.” “Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. stories.description: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends • The best eco-friendly baby products Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need. There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. Many are also wifi-enabled, meaning you can connect the monitor to your smartphone and view the live feed through an app instead of using a dedicated parent unit (read on for security advice). stories.description: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years. Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains. Continue reading...

stories.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
stories.description: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles. stories.description: This live blog is now closed. Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win Sign up for the Breaking News US email The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other , according to the New York Times. The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors. A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed. The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role. The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December . Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race. Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference. Continue reading...

stories.title: Election date? Brexit reset outcome? Farage’s survival chances? Andrew Sparrow answered readers questions
stories.description: The Guardian’s UK politics blogger answered readers’ questions These are from my colleague Peter Walker , who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor. Peter posted this before the result was announced. Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport. Cleverly says he would “end Khan’s war on motorists”, which is a sign he might lean into the anti-cycling and walking rhetoric which the London Tories have a habit of espousing. Expect talk about LTNs and 20mph zones. In the media Q&A Cleverly is pinned down on whether he backs the Tory party line on wanting to leave the ECHR and opposes net zero. He confirms he does (as he has to). Such things will be ready ammunition for Labour. Cleverly says of Andy Burnham, “His residual behaviour is to be anti-London”. This will very much be a theme of his campaign, it seems. Not sure how resonant a “poor London!” message will be even in London People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related. The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. Continue reading...

stories.description: Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit Tories select James Cleverly as candidate for London mayor Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”. As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024 . A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip. Continue reading...

It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Continue reading...

stories.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
stories.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. The Game Boy itself used a slow, old Sharp LR35902 processor and a sickly green monochrome screen, but it also came with Tetris and worked for ages on four AA batteries. With sales of 65m, it was vastly more successful than hi-tech rivals such as the Atari Lynx and Sega Game Gear. Continue reading...

But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech. Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. stories.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
stories.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. stories.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
stories.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. For example, when I set off the alarm at a glinting modernist abode, I had to quickly dodge the gunshot fired my way by its maniacal owner, and as I scarpered across the surrounding grassy verge, I grabbed underpants off the clothesline just to make the long drive through the night worth it. I was reminded of Shameless (the US version) as much as Steinbeck. Continue reading...

stories.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...

I don’t believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain. I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years. And actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016. People’s jobs depend on working together and collaborating. And that’s our approach, and it will always be our approach. People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are. Look, here’s my starting point. My constituents, people across the country, voted for a range of reasons for Brexit, but one of them was one of the biggest, certainly for my constituents, was to make our economy better, positive economic change. stories.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
stories.description: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones. stories.description: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight. The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks. UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent , which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds. Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march. UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police . West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward. Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance . The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage. Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released. Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia. stories.title: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain - as it happened
stories.description: Iran has targeted airbase in Bahrain in latest resumption of strikes since september The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples. The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression against its territory, including the attack launched today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, by drones that were intercepted and destroyed by air defense systems in the Kingdom’s airspace. This comes two days after a similar attack at dawn on Friday, November 13, 2026, by two drones that were also intercepted. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression. The Ministry considered these attacks a resumption of Iran’s heinous aggression against the Kingdom and countries in the region , disregarding the provisions of international law and the principles of the UN Charter. stories.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

stories.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
stories.description: The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. That includes Cornell University , Penn State University , Elgin Community College , Emory University , Binghamton University , Kent State University and the University of Wisconsin’s Madison , Milwaukee and Oshkosh branches. stories.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
stories.description: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia. After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP. Continue reading...

stories.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
stories.description: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”. stories.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
stories.description: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies. Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines. You are either excited that the news might be a signal of a long overdue romcom resurgence, or you are embittered because it’s another sign that Hollywood has run out of original ideas. I hold absolutely no truck with the latter view. Quite frankly, if there was ever a film in dire need of a reboot, then it’s You’ve Got Mail. The film is almost 28 years old, and it shows every single day of its age. You’ve seen it, you know how it goes. It’s about two people who use the futuristic new technology of email (email is no longer new) to communicate, despite being rival booksellers ( nobody reads books any more ), and eventually begin a relationship ( nobody wants to be in a relationship any more ). stories.title: Even Martin Scorsese uses AI for storyboards. Can the art survive?
stories.description: As Hollywood begins to adopt the technology, the professionals in most direct jeopardy are the illustrators mapping out directors’ first visions. They sketch out what could be lost A film industry dominated by AI is a dystopian prospect: stories and dialogue generated by large language models, populated by reincarnated screen icons and uncanny humanoids . That is in the future, but the real-world impact of AI is already directly affecting jobs behind the scenes, as Hollywood’s biggest film-makers begin to adopt the technology. James Cameron – long an advocate for emerging technologies in film-making – is on the board of a gen AI firm , citing his interest in how AI will intersect with CGI; Steven Soderbergh used Meta-powered tech to create animations for his recent documentary about John Lennon ; even Christopher Nolan, while dismissing the idea that AI will replace humans as “nonsense”, conceded that it will create some useful “imaging tools”. The current canary in the coalmine however is the storyboard artist, whose work gen AI appears to have directly in its sights. Storyboard artists are the illustrators who draw the panels of images with notes and diagrams that map out scenes before they are filmed. Storyboards are used to work out how a film will look, and as a blueprint to communicate a director’s vision to cast and crew , and are one of the first steps in bringing a script off the page. Now they appear on the verge of replacement by programmes that use text prompts to create illustrations instead. Even an old-school diehard like Martin Scorsese has got on board; in June he announced a partnership with an AI firm whose text-to-image model he used in the storyboarding process for his next movie. stories.description: The chipmaker faces business risks and political scrutiny due to its over-reliance on founder and CEO Jensen Huang Why is Nvidia’s Jensen Huang at the centre of a US-China row? Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal . The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power. Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US. stories.description: We can’t allow our health data to be locked into the control of a US tech firm. It won’t be easy, but next spring the job of clawing it back must begin Ben Coleman is Labour MP for Chelsea and Fulham and a member of the health and social care committee Next March, Palantir’s £330m contract to run NHS England’s federated data platform (FDP) ends. Ministers must decide by Christmas whether to extend it. They should move on from Palantir, and transition to new suppliers that put the NHS in full control of its technology and patient data. I sit on the health and social care committee. In June, we recommended no extension – people don’t trust Palantir , its benefits are contested and other tools could deliver the same or similar advantages. The debate so far has been whether to drop Palantir. The harder question is what replaces it. The tempting solution is to hire a single British firm. But that would not give the NHS the control it lacks: the freedom to switch supplier without losing what it has built. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn. As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. stories.title: Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option | Elisabeth Braw
stories.description: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe. Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World Continue reading...
